questions.title: Clinical Recognition of Jaundice
questions.correctedQuestion: At approximately what total bilirubin level does jaundice usually become clinically apparent?

correctedOptions.A: About 2–3 mg/dL
correctedOptions.C: It may result from hemolysis or hepatobiliary disease

correctAnswer.text: A — Clinically seen if total bilirubin > 5

questions.explanation: The source threshold is too high; the question also contains too few options.

correctedAnswer.text: A — About 2–3 mg/dL

questions.whyCorrectedAnswer: Jaundice, particularly scleral icterus, is usually clinically detectable when the serum total bilirubin is approximately 2–3 mg/dL. The original value of >5 mg/dL is higher than the usual clinical threshold.
questions.correctedExplanation: The original question is poorly worded and contains an incorrect/overly high bilirubin threshold. The corrected version clarifies the intended clinical concept and distinguishes the usual threshold for visible jaundice from the original wording.

correctionDetails.whatWasCorrected: The question wording was rewritten for clarity, the spelling of bilirubin was corrected, the clinical threshold was corrected to approximately 2–3 mg/dL, and the incomplete option set was reconstructed for study purposes.
correctionDetails.why: The original wording is abbreviated and the stated >5 mg/dL threshold is higher than the usual level at which jaundice becomes clinically apparent.
correctionDetails.medicalInformation: Visible jaundice/scleral icterus is generally detectable at approximately 2–3 mg/dL total serum bilirubin; the exact visibility threshold can vary with examination conditions and patient factors.
